title: Curious what animation software/workflows you all use
author: sfst4i45fwe
selftext:
I would like to know how you all animate your characters (not just human motion, anything).

Have any of you tried using third party software along with AI (using MCP or CLI)? Or do you just prompt the LLM to animate for you using whatever language your game is in?

comments.author: TreasureChestylicius
comments.body: yo uso aseprite, es un poco dificil de hacer animaciones, quisiera ver como funciona pixelLab parece bueno.

comments.author: Ok_Feedback4200
comments.body:
If you are serious about animation, want full control and have awesome fucking animations, then learn Cascadeur. It's not expensive and it's very easy to learn. You don't need to be an animator. It can be used with custom riggs not just humanoids.

Claude alone won't give you good character animations, or you'll need to build a proper documented workflow which it can follow in detail.. If you expect a propmt = character animation, check out kimodo and how to run it offline on your gpu. But it's only for humanoids for now. It's pretty much Mixamo 2.0 now... Original Mixamo has been used for more than a decade now probably. It will still give you better animations for characters than what Claude on MCP could animate from a prompt...

comments.author: _HoundOfJustice
comments.body: I use Autodesk Maya for animation, its the industry standard for good reasons. It even has its own AI tools like ML deformer and genAI one that is Motionmaker which is for motion also allows custom data to be trained on. I also rely on to me non negotiable add ons that are Animbot and mGear (or Advanced Skeleton). I use Claude to make custom MEL and Python tools for Maya as well as custom tools for mGear to make rigging a better and more automated experience.

comments.author: stolenyourgf
comments.body:
For 2D pixel stuff I still animate in Aseprite: key poses first, then in-betweens with onion skin, one tag per state (idle/run/attack). Then the Aseprite CLI exports everything in one go:  
aseprite -b char.aseprite --sheet char.png --data char.json --format json-array --list-tags  
That's where AI is actually useful for me: having it write the importer that turns the JSON tags into engine animations. Letting it generate the frames themselves still gives too much drift between frames.
